response: That premise is backwards. Git rebase on shared branches is explicitly unsafe—it rewrites history that others have already pulled, forcing them to deal with messy conflicts and synchronization problems. That's the core reason merge commits exist: they preserve how the work actually happened without rewriting shared history. Use rebase for local branches before pushing; use merge for shared work.

No. Payment code has zero margin for error. A bug here means fraud, data loss, or customer refund chaos—the blast radius is massive. Even for small, well-understood modules in critical paths, tests are non-negotiable. The cost of a single bug far exceeds the time to write tests. "I understand it well" isn't sufficient confidence for payment logic.

I'm not hedging—correlation and causation are statistically different things. Your A/B numbers show correlation (the group with the feature experienced lift), but other factors could have caused it: selection bias, timing effects, a concurrent marketing push, seasonal trends, or measurement error. To claim causation, you need to rule those out. What does your experimental design actually control for?

That premise isn't established. Research shows sleep deprivation does harm most people's cognitive performance, even those adapted to it. Some individuals show more resilience, but "sleep under six hours has no effect" is overstated. Before optimizing your schedule on that claim, share your sources—I'd want to see the actual studies and their sample sizes and control groups.

That's a popular myth with no scientific basis. Neuroscientists use fMRI, PET scans, EEG, and direct electrode recording—they all show most of the brain is active nearly all the time, even during sleep. We use far more than 10% of our brain. The myth might stem from misquoted statements about conscious awareness or untapped potential, but the "idle 90%" isn't how neurobiology works.

This creates serious risk. You lose scaling (can't scale database and web independently when one becomes the bottleneck), isolation (runaway queries starve the web server, traffic spikes starve the database), resilience (one failure brings down both), and observability (harder to diagnose whether problems are compute, memory, I/O, or network). This usually backfires when load increases. What's your actual traffic profile and growth projection?

You're both partly right, and your lawyer friend is wrong on the legal standard. GDPR applies based on processing EU residents' personal data, not where your company is incorporated. If your US company processes data belonging to EU residents (email, location, behavior, etc.), GDPR applies to you—regardless of your location or incorporation. The question isn't "Are we a US company?" It's "Do we process EU residents' data?"

TypeScript is a static type checker, not runtime safety. It catches type errors at compile time, but can't catch: logic errors (your code does the wrong thing), async failures or unhandled promise rejections, errors from external APIs, or malformed data at runtime. Apps crash because of logic bugs, edge cases, or dependency failures—not type errors. TypeScript makes some bug classes less likely, but it's not comprehensive protection.
